entities.name: Abel Aubert Dupetit Thouars
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Vice-Admiral Abel Aubert du Petit-Thouars (1793–1864) was a pivotal figure in 19th-century French naval expansion, whose decisive actions in the Pacific Ocean fundamentally reshaped the geopolitical map of Oceania and solidified France's imperial presence. Born into a distinguished naval family, his career spanned the Napoleonic Wars through the mid-19th century, culminating in his command of the French Pacific Squadron and his instrumental role in the establishment of the French Protectorate over Tahiti. His strategic maneuvers were a direct manifestation of France's burgeoning colonial ambitions under King Louis-Philippe I, positioning him at the forefront of European powers' competition for influence in the vast Pacific. 

In 1842, commanding the frigate *La Reine Blanche*, Dupetit Thouars arrived in Tahiti amidst local political turmoil and growing Protestant missionary influence, particularly from Great Britain. Seizing an opportunity presented by internal disputes and appeals from Tahitian Catholic missionaries, he compelled Queen Pōmare IV to sign a treaty establishing a French Protectorate over the island on September 9, 1842. Two years later, following the Pritchard Affair – a diplomatic incident involving British consul George Pritchard – Dupetit Thouars unilaterally deposed Queen Pōmare IV and declared Tahiti a French colony on November 6, 1843, though this full annexation was later partially reversed to a protectorate by the French government under British diplomatic pressure.
